prize_parts.citation: For the optical lattice clock: the magic-wavelength lattice that lets many neutral atoms be interrogated without shifting the clock transition, and its realisation at fractional uncertainties near 10^-18.

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from KPZ (B056) to optical lattice clocks (B002), and I want to say plainly why. My objection in round 1 was that a clock is an ever more accurate instrument in a lineage already honoured in 2005 and 2012. The replies make a distinction I find convincing on the physics. The comb is a ruler for optical frequencies, and the 2012 prize concerned control of single quantum systems. The magic-wavelength lattice is a different kind of idea: choose the trapping wavelength at which the differential light shift of the two clock levels vanishes, so a perturbing trap becomes harmless. This is the kind of simple, general mechanism I normally look for, and it turns a single-particle measurement into a many-atom one with a statistical gain. It was then reproduced and surpassed by several independent laboratories (RIKEN and Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE), and it has produced new observations: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, many-body effects in the clock, and constraints on varying constants and dark-matter couplings. Every member who names a pair names Katori and Ye, so the credit does not need to be argued around a collaboration or a split between theory and experiment. Maturity is not in doubt. The citation should rest on what has been demonstrated and make no claim about a redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: Two points weigh on me and neither is settled. First, the discovery-versus-technique question: I accept that the lattice regime is new, but the committee has not agreed a single sentence that says what B002 recognises and the 2005 and 2012 prizes did not, and without that sentence the citation can be read as a third prize in one lineage. Second, priority. Nobody in the round-1 files has checked the early-2000s record on who proposed the magic-wavelength idea first (Katori, and the parallel proposals of Pottier, Lemonde and others), or how credit divides between Katori's first demonstration and Ye's accuracy records, as Olsson asks. Lemonde, Takamoto and the Sr and Yb community remain outside the two names. On KPZ itself, which I now hold as an alternative and not as my first choice, the weaknesses I listed stand: Parisi and the authors of the exact solutions are outside the credited names, and the experimental confirmation rests mostly on one liquid-crystal system.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a ruler and the 2012 prize rewarded single-ion control, whereas Katori solved how to trap thousands of atoms without shifting the transition, which gives the statistical gain behind 10^-18. She also says the KPZ confirmation is mostly from one liquid-crystal system.
responses.response: This is the argument that changed my mind. I had treated the lattice clock as a refinement. The vanishing differential light shift at the magic wavelength is a mechanism, and the many-atom statistics follow from it, so the content is distinct from the two earlier prizes. Her test of reproduction across many laboratories is also fair, and B002 passes it much more clearly than B056. On her KPZ point I partly disagree: Takeuchi and Sano's turbulent liquid-crystal data were later complemented by other growth experiments, but those are less clean, and I do not claim the breadth of reproduction that the clocks have. I now accept that on this criterion B002 is the stronger case.

responses.point: Kroll asks me to say what the discovery in B056 is that is independent of the 1986 theory, since Takeuchi's experiment is the part that must be tested for reproducibility and the exact-solution authors are outside the credited names. He also separates subject adjacency from content overlap for the clocks.
responses.response: The part of B056 independent of the 1986 theory is the measurement of the full distribution of height fluctuations and its Tracy-Widom form in a real system. That result is genuine, but the exact solutions that made the prediction precise were by others, and the independent confirmations are fewer than I implied, so his challenge largely holds. His distinction between subject adjacency and content overlap is right, and it is the reason I withdraw the overlap objection to B002. I keep one request from him and Lindroth: the committee should record the early-2000s chronology of the magic-wavelength proposals before the citation is fixed.

responses.point: Olsson applies the criterion that the prize goes to the original experiment and not to the second group that did it much better, and asks that the priority between Katori and Ye be reviewed. She also says she cannot tell whether Takeuchi's experiment is the original result for KPZ.
responses.response: I share the criterion, and it applies to my own first choice as much as to B002. For B002 I read the roles as complementary: Katori proposed the lattice scheme and made the first strontium clock, and Ye's group made it the accuracy and stability benchmark. Both are creditable parts of one achievement, provided the citation names the magic-wavelength lattice and not clocks in general. If the chronology check shows Ye's lattice work was independent of Katori's proposal, I would want that recorded. For KPZ, the lesson from her question is that the experimental credit is itself ambiguous, which is one more reason I no longer put B056 first.

responses.point: Johansson says the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is smaller than it looks, that the lattice combines many neutral atoms with a magic wavelength, and that a citation should not promise a redefinition of the second. He would not oppose waiting if a clearer result were imminent.
responses.response: I agree on the citation: it should rest on demonstrated performance, the redshift measurement and the fundamental-physics tests. I would not wait. Thorium and ion clocks are not close enough to alter what has been shown by lattice clocks, and waiting for a redefinition would tie a prize to a metrological decision rather than to science. His remark that support comes from members in very different fields carries weight with me, but only because those members gave scientific reasons that I tested against the physics, and I do not count it as support.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators (B015) as a theory-plus-experiment discovery of a new phase of matter, confirmed across HgTe, InAs/GaSb and 3D materials, and regards it as arguably overdue.
responses.response: I still rate the physics highly, and B015 remains close behind my first choice on science. My difficulty has not changed. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (deceased) and the 3D contributors Fu, Moore, Hasan and Cava are outside the trio, and the 2016 prize already covered topological phases in part, so the committee would have to argue lineage and attribution at once. On the chair's question about a second part, no remaining candidate would fit within a three-person limit alongside B002 without that difficulty, so I propose B002 alone.

uncertainties: Priority for the magic-wavelength lattice in the early 2000s (Katori versus parallel proposals) and the division of credit between Katori's first demonstration and Ye's accuracy records; I have not seen the original papers in this exchange.
Whether the committee will agree a precise sentence on what B002 recognises that the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize did not.
Whether KPZ (B056) could be completed with a defensible set of names once Parisi and the exact-solution authors are outside the limit; I regard this as unlikely but am not certain.
Whether a second distinct achievement is needed. With a three-person ceiling I see no clean pairing with B002.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict: none of my frequent co-authors is among the credited names for any shortlisted candidate, and I have no tie to Katori or Ye. My random-matrix background is intellectually close to the exact KPZ solutions (B056), which is now an alternative and not my preferred part. I share a Gothenburg physics environment with Johansson and Olsson (Chalmers), but I know of no collaboration with them or with the circuit-QED community. I noted Olsson's University of Tokyo fellowship and Kroll's JILA background as disclosed institutional connections to B002, and I take both as stated.
